title: Move `master` branch to `main`
description:
Cc @t-kalinowski

The `master` branch of this repository will soon be renamed to `main`, as part of a coordinated change across several GitHub organizations (including, but not limited to: [tidyverse](https://github.com/tidyverse), [r-lib](https://github.com/r-lib), [tidymodels](https://github.com/tidymodels), and [sol-eng](https://github.com/sol-eng)). We anticipate this will happen by the end of September 2021.

That will be preceded by a release of the [usethis package](https://usethis.r-lib.org), which will gain some functionality around detecting and adapting to a renamed default branch. There will also be a blog post at the time of this `master` --> `main` change.

The purpose of this issue is to:

* Help us firm up the list of targetted repositories
* Make sure all maintainers are aware of what's coming
* Give us an issue to close when the job is done
* Give us a place to put advice for collaborators re: how to adapt

*message id: entire_lizard*

title: `tfruns` reports wrong metrics when using early stopping
description:
When using `tfruns` with `callbacks = callback_early_stopping(patience = 4, restore_best_weights = TRUE)` , a "wrong" set of results are reported since metrics come from the last epoch, when in fact the weights of the models are restored from a different epoch. Needless to say that the longer the patience, the more likely that your results may drastically differ.

![Untitled](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/47745523/120857721-0083f380-c582-11eb-8b10-4b95806f57d6.png)

This could be "manually" checked for a single run, but it is misleading when reviewing many runs (`ls_runs()`) and the choice of the best hyperparameters.

title: Error when testing different number of layers?
description:
Hi, 

love the package, and I have a decent handle on it for tuning most parameters.

However, is it possible to tune how many layers to add in a model?

Say I want to test between 1 and 2 layers in a simple LSTM model example. I tune the units and dropout rate for both layers when included, and always the learning rate.
However, I want the tuning run to test runs where it drops/includes the 2nd layer. 
How can I achieve this in tfruns?

Example of how I tried to do it with strings and a logical statement:

In file where I run the tuning_run() function:
```
testruns <-tuning_run("lstmmod.R",
                       flags = list(lr = c(0.01, 0.005),
                                    u1 = c(32,64), #units layer 1
                                    u2 = c(16), #units layer 2
                                    d1 = c(0.1), #dropout rate layer 1
                                    d2 = c(0.1), #dropout rate layer 2
                                    exl = c("TRUE","FALSE"))) # In the model file I use an if statement with exl == "TRUE"
```
In the model file:
```
FLAGS <- flags(flag_numeric('learn', 0.01),
               flag_numeric('un1',64),
               flag_numeric('un2',32),
               flag_numeric('dr1',0.1),
               flag_numeric('dr2',0.1),
               flag_string('exl', "TRUE"))


# Specify model
model <- keras_model_sequential()
model %>%
  layer_lstm(units=FLAGS$u1, return_sequences = T, dropout = FLAGS$d1)

if(exl == "TRUE") {
  model %>% 
  layer_lstm(units=FLAGS$u2, return_sequences = F, recurrent_dropout = FLAGS$d2)
}

model %>% 
  layer_dense(units=length_sequence) %>%
  compile(loss="mse", optimizer=optimizer_adam(lr = FLAGS$learn))

history <- model %>% fit(x_train, y_train, validation_data=(x_val,y_val), epochs=50)
```
This failed.

Any help would be appreciated, the key issue is simply how I'd formulate this since the if thing failed.

title: [Scope Extension] Please make tfrun available for mlverse/torch runs
tuning_run appears to mishandle dataframes for the flag parameter
description:
The tuning run function appears to call expand.grid on all data.frames that enter through the `flags` argument.

A quick reproducible example:

a file named 'nnet-unit.R' lives in a directory called 'codedir' - its contents are as follows

```
#flags for tuning_run
FLAGS = flags(
	flag_numeric('width1', 16),
	flag_numeric('dropout', .1)
)

#sequentially build model


model = keras_model_sequential() %>% 
                layer_dense(units = 1, activation = 'linear', input_shape = c(num_zs)) %>%
	        layer_dense(units = FLAGS$width1, input_shape = c(num_zs, activation = 
                              'relu')) %>% layer_dropout(rate = FLAGS$dropout)

#regression problem here so send to linear activation function with 1 unit...
	
model %>% layer_dense(units = 1, activation = 'linear')}



compile(model, optimizer = 'adam', loss = 'mse')

history = model %>% fit(x = train_dat, y =train_lab, epochs = 40, batch_size= 10, verbose = 0)

evaluate(model, test_dat, test_lab, verbose = 0)

k_clear_session()

```

is called from a `tuning_run()` where

`flags = data.frame(dropout = c(0,.1, .15, .2), width1= c(16,32,64,128))`

the final call would be 

`tuning_run(here('codedir', 'nnet-unit.R'), runs_dir = here("tuningdir", 'tunename'), flags = flags,
                confirm = FALSE, echo = FALSE)`

documentation would suggest that the tuning_run would tune over 4 models, but currently it appears to tune over 16. This is also true when there are repeated values in the flags df - that is, if flags were:

`flags = data.frame(dropout = c(0, 0, 0, .1), width = c(32, 64, 128, 32))` tuning_run will still tune over 16 models.

Any guidance as to how to tune over only the models specified in a 'flags' dataframe?

Thank you!

title: Control dimensions of plots saved during training
description:
When the training script contains a small plot, it's neatly displayed in the window opened by `view_run()`, but in my particular case the plot I'd like to look at is a little busy with multiple facets, therefore needing a bigger size so I can actually make something out.

My current workaround is to manually save the plot (I've tried both `ggsave` and manual `png(...) <...> dev.off()`), which does the trick regarding adjustable dimensions, but it comes at a cost:

I have not yet quite figured out the paths used during plotting – it looks like plots are saved in my project root by default and then copied (*not* moved because they remain there) to the run's directory (but then again, _not_ in the `plots` directory.

Before I dive deeper into paths and environments, I'd rather ask: Is there a better way to plot at larger dimensions without having to explicitly save the plots?

Thus, my request/question: Is it possible to log the tfrun FLAGS such that they are available as HParams in the tensorboard dashboard?

title: option to include additional files in the sources.tar.gz saved by training_run
Unexplicable errors when sample ratio is too low
description:
If you set the sample ratio too low, it's possible to sample zero rows, and then you get weird, unhelpful error messages about NA values:

```r
tfruns::tuning_run("path/to/model", flags = list(RFM_UNITS_1 = 1), sample = 1e-6)
```

results in:

```
Error: Unable to convert flag 'RFM_UNITS_1' with value 'NA' to type integer
```

This can be solved by:

* always returning at least one row of the sampling grid if `sample > 0`
* throwing a helpful error if `sample <= 0`

PR coming soon.

title: Allow passing a DOE to tuning_run
description:
`tuning_run` is amazing, and I'm stress-testing it right now with a whopping ~1300 runs :smile: However, the fact that only full factorial DOEs or random sampling DOEs are possible is quite limiting, for people who don't have access to big GPU clusters. For example, have a look at my flag list:

```r
runs <- tuning_run("fit_single_model.R", flags = list(
  hidden_units = c(64, 128, 256, 512),
  activation_function = c("relu", "tanh", "elu"),
  batch_norm = c(FALSE, TRUE),
  dropout = c(0.0, 0.3, 0.5),
  use_adam = c(TRUE, FALSE),
  learning_rate = c(0.001, 0.0001, 0.01),
  batch_size = c(32, 64, 128)
))
```

It clearly doesn't make sense to run Adam with the largest initial learning rates, which instead make sense when `use_adam = FALSE` (in that case my code uses Nesterov SGD + a learning rate scheduler). In the same way, runs with large batch size and small initial learning rate don't seem a brilliant idea.

----

Now, of course to allow for conditional hyperparameter tuning (i.e., make the ranges of some hyperparameters depend on the values of others), like in [hyperopt](https://github.com/hyperopt/hyperopt ), would require too much work and I'm not asking for that. But why don't you allow us to pass a DOE to `tuning_run`? This way, you kill two pigeons with one stone:

- you give the user total freedom in specifying exactly which combinations of hp will be run...
- ... but you also offload to her/him the effort involved in designing a DOE "which makes sense", i.e., which excludes nonsensical combinations of hyperparameters.

I _think_ that should be a relatively low effort/high reward modification.

title: Using tuning_run to experiment with neural network architecture
description:
I was experimenting with using `tuning_run` to collect data on the performance of models with different numbers of hidden layers, and I wanted to ask about some of the issues that came up. Currently, tfrun requires flags of length one and has stringent requirements on the form of the hyperparameter subspace to search - i.e. it can only search (possibly random subsets of) the space of all combinations of values specified in individual vectors for each flag. This makes it difficult to use `tuning_run` to experiment with different numbers of hidden layers and different numbers of units in each hidden layer. First, is there any downside to using `tuning_run` in this way? Is it more commonly used to optimize simpler parameters?

The most natural way I can think of to control the number of hidden layers and hidden units through flags is to have a single single flag which is a vector of integers which gives the number of units for each layer. Since flags need to be length one, another approach is to use an integer flag `num_hidden_layers` for the number of hidden layers, and flags `hidden_units_1`, `hidden_units_2`, etc for the number of hidden units in each layer. The problem then is that you don't want to execute multiple training runs where `num_hidden_layers` is constant and `hidden_units_x` changes but isn't used. You can probably get around this by using an `if` statement in your model script to not fit the model in these cases. Or you can get around the problem altogether by parameterizing the number of hidden layers and number of units in each layer by a single integer flag, which isn't hard but is unnatural and hard to read.

Anyways, I think this raises some more general issues. Sometimes, as in the case of `hidden_units_x` and `num_hidden_layers` above, flags are naturally nested in other flags. As another example, someone might use a learning rate flag and an optimizer flag and only want to try certain values of learning rate for a certain optimizer. Any thoughts on this? These issues could probably be solved by introducing a way to specify your own set of parameter combinations to try, as in https://github.com/rstudio/tfruns/issues/30. Maybe the user could specify a data frame of flags, with one column per flag. Would you be interested in a pull request with a feature like this?

title: Worse performance with more files in working directory
description:
`training_run()` scans the whole working directory for changes in `with_changed_file_copy()` which has (in my case) significant performance implications. 

https://github.com/rstudio/tfruns/blob/master/R/training_run.R#L228

In what sense is that necessary? It seems sensible to me to limit this to the directory of the training script, which I implemented in my [fork](https://github.com/lorenzwalthert/tfruns/tree/performance). However, I am not sure about dependencies of this part of the code. What's your opinion? Alternatively, we could introduce an argument (which defaults to a global option) to handle which files are scanned.

title: (lower-level) API for specifying grid in tuning_run()
description:
It has happened to me a few times that a grid search with `tuning_run()` was aborted unexpectedly. If one wants to evaluate the full grid, it is relatively tedious to find out which parameter combinations were evaluated already and then continue from there. I imagine a change to the API so the user could also 

* Provide a grid (instead of the parameter combinations used to create a grid) to `tuning_run()`.
* Retrieve evaluated combinations from some file which is updated after every completed iteration.
* Remove the evaluated parameter combinations from the grid using the information from the bullet above.
* Complete the grid search, evaluating only options that were not already evaluated.

What do you think of this functionality?

title: Smart hyper-parameter tuning
description: This package is very useful, thanks. I am currently spending a lot of time on hyper-parameter tuning for neural nets and I've been using `tfruns::tuning_run()` with (random) grid search. Are there any plans to include *intelligent* methods for hyper-parameter tuning, i.e. based on Bayesian optimization?

title: enforcing types on flags?
description:
If you have a `flags.yml` containing e.g.

```
default:
    numeric: "whoops",
    boolean: "bad-parameter"
```

And a flags declaration:

```
FLAGS <- flags(
    flag_numeric("numeric", 0),
    flag_boolean("boolean", FALSE)
)
```

The `flags()` invocation succeeds, but with a warning:

```
> flags(
+     flag_numeric("numeric", 0),
+     flag_boolean("boolean", FALSE)
+ )
Warning in parse_flags(FLAGS, config, file, arguments) :
  NAs introduced by coercion
    name    type value description
 numeric numeric    NA          NA
 boolean boolean    NA          NA
```

I wonder if this should instead be an error?

title: allow undeclared parameters in 'flags()' call?
description:
In some initial bits of porting from the old config-based approach to the tfruns flags approach, I saw errors of the form:

```
Error: The following flags were provided but not declared: eval_num_epochs, eval_batch_size, eval_delay_secs, eval_steps, train_num_epochs, train_batch_size, train_steps
```

Should we consider silently allowing these fields? It does seem a bit unfortunate that one must effectively duplicate the declarations between the `flags()` command invocation and the `flags.yml` configuration(s). It might be nice for some workflows to just allow a plain old:

```
FLAGS <- flags()
```

and just populate all the flags as discovered in `flags.yml` (and overlay whatever options are specified on the command line). There's probably a reason why this approach wasn't taken but just want to be sure.
